data.title: The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Scripts rise for Foundayo, Wegovy pill
data.description:
With the recent launches of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo, the obesity market has started to shift toward oral GLP-1 drugs. While Novo leverages its first-mover advantage with the familiar Wegovy brand, Lilly is betting that the freedom from strict fasting and water requirements can give Foundayo an edge.

Each week, Fierce Pharma’s Oral GLP-1 Tracker will leverage analysts’ notes and IQVIA data to monitor prescription trends and shifting market shares as these two titans vie to become the go-to oral weight-loss solution for millions.

UPDATED: Oct. 30, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill ticked back up last week, although neither matched previous records.

Foundayo enjoyed 63,110 total scripts in its 29th week of launch, still shy of the 64,268 record set in week 25, according IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

Wegovy pill's roughly 183K scrips also came slightly below the 184K height it had briefly reached five weeks ago. During the week, the oral version constituted 36% of all Wegovy scripts.

Approximately every 4 in 10 patients starting an oral obesity medicine choose Foundayo, and the number of new Foundayo patients in the third quarter doubled from the previous quarter, Lilly's CFO said on the company's Q3 earnings call Thursday.

In Q3, Foundayo sales reached $184 million, missing consensus estimates by $50 million, according to a Jefferies note. including $124 million from the U.S. Still, Lilly's stock price jumped during Thursday's earnings report, "which to us suggests investors are increasingly focusing on the breadth and depth of [Lilly]'s obesity franchise rather than near-term Foundayo [numbers]," Jefferies' analysts said. Sales from both of Lilly's tirzepatide products, Mounjaro and Zepbound, came above Wall Street's projections during Q3.

UPDATED: Oct. 23, 2026

Last week’s federal holiday, Columbus Day, led to an unsurprising dip for prescriptions of both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 rival Foundayo in the U.S. 

In the prior-week reporting period, Novo’s Wegovy pill saw prescriptions fall slightly to around 173K versus the 173.5K tallied the week ending Oct. 9, according to Citi and Jefferies analysts, both of whom leverage prescribing data from IQVIA. 

For that same period, prescriptions of Eli Lilly’s GLP-1 pill Foundayo slipped around 4% week over week to 58K. 

The minor reversal for both drugs shouldn’t come as a surprise, given that national holidays are liable to impact weekly prescribing trends. 

Looking at the broader oral GLP-1 market, Lilly’s share presently sits a little higher than 25%, according to the Jefferies team, while Novo holds a nearly 75% piece of the pie. 

Meanwhile, as Novo and Lilly vie over the ever-important U.S. obesity market, the GLP-1 opportunity taking shape across other massive countries like China, India and Brazil could grow from $6.6 billion now to a whopping $22 billion by the middle of the next decade, according to a new J.P. Morgan estimate reported by Reuters Friday. 

UPDATED: Oct. 16, 2026

The previous week was rather uneventful for the two oral GLP-1 drugs as Americans geared up for another national holiday, Columbus Day.

Total prescriptions for Novo's Wegovy pill dipped about 3% sequentially to approximately 173.5K last week. Again, the script number was the result of a compromise between Citi's reported 173K and Jefferies' 174K, both referencing IQVIA.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo scripts ticked up about 4% to 60,151, still shy of the small molecule's previous record of 64,268.

In the broader obesity market, Lilly's Zepbound remained the leader with about 801.8K total scripts, relatively flat week over week. All Wegovy scripts across its injectable and oral forms trended 2.5% downward and landed at about 492.6K, according to Citi.

Earlier this week, drug regulators at the European Medicines Agency recommended a marketing authorization in the European Union for Foundayo for both weight management and Type 2 diabetes in adults. The European Commission is expected to sign off on the approval in a few weeks. 

UPDATED: Oct. 9, 2026

Prescriptions for Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill pulled back a little during the last week. 

In its 26th week of launch, Foundayo achieved 57,920 total scripts, down 9.9% sequentially, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

For oral Wegovy, Citi said IQVIA recorded roughly 179K scripts, while Jefferies quoted 180K. To reconcile the discrepancy between the two numbers, we used 179.5K, which translates into a 1.4% weekly decline.

In fact, scripts for all major GLP-1s declined last week across diabetes and obesity care, save for Lilly's Zepbound KwikPen, a prefilled injection pen that delivers four fixed weekly doses of tirzepatide, according to Jefferies. Overall Zepbound scripts dipped below 800K in a 0.8% decrease sequentially, just as Novo's total Wegovy scripts fell 2.7% to 505.5K, according to Citi.

Based on the numbers, Jefferies now models $208 million for Foundayo sales in the third quarter, which the team noted is in line with consensus.

UPDATED: Oct. 2, 2026

Eli Lilly's Foundayo is showing clearer signs of acceleration. Total prescriptions for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist surged about 21% to 64,268 during last week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. That haul came off a 13% sequential increase the week before that.

"We're seeing early signs of growth in Q3 for Foundayo," Jefferies analysts wrote in an Oct. 2 note.

Recent expansion of Foundayo could be attributed to a direct-to-consumer ad first aired in late August featuring Martha Stewart, as well as the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program which, as of July, offers eligible seniors GLP-1 obesity drugs at a $50 monthly copay.

Meanwhile, Novo's Wegovy pill scripts appear stuck at just above $180K. Except for a Labor Day holiday lull, total weekly scripts for the oral semaglutide product have hovered between 181K and 184K over the past five weeks, including 182K last week, according to Citi.

It's worth noting that Foundayo took 25 weeks to reach what the Wegovy pill achieved in just seven weeks in terms of total scripts. But the gap between the two drugs is closing. As Jefferies noted, Lilly owned 26% of the oral obesity market as of last week, versus a little less than 23% in the previous two weeks.

Overall, Lilly's Zepbound remains the obesity market leader with total scripts of 805.7K, up 2.3% sequentially, according to Citi. Novo's total Wegovy scripts for the pill and the injectable were down 0.6% sequentially to a 519.6K.

At the European Association for the Study of Diabetes annual meeting in Milan earlier this week, both Lilly and Novo rolled out multiple data sets touting the blood-sugar, weight-loss, cardiovascular benefits of their GLP-1 programs amid a wave of potential challengers.

UPDATED: Sept. 25, 2026

Total prescriptions for both Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill have bounced back following a holiday dip and reached new records. Weekly scripts for the Wegov pill jumped 14% sequentially to about 184K, compared with its previous high of 183K, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. Foundayo climbed 13% to cross 50K for the first time, reaching 53,321.

Foundayo now captures about 1 out of 3 new starts for oral GLP-1 obesity drugs, and “that’s growing week over week,” Lilly CEO David Ricks told CNBC in an interview this week. 

As Leerink Partners analysts noted in a Sept. 23 note, effective Sept. 1, Lilly cut the initial-dose pricing for Foundayo 0.8 mg, 2.5 mg and 5.5 mg to $149, $149 and $199 per month for self-pay patients, respectively. The company framed the promotion as an elasticity experiment and as a push to the first maintenance dose, according to the Leerink note.

As Jefferies analysts pointed out in a Sept. 25 note, the majority of Foundayo scripts seem to be cash pay, with about 80% of patients still on starting doses.

Based on the IQVIA data so far, the Jefferies team estimated U.S. Foundayo revenues of $203 million in the third quarter, slightly lower than the $209 million consensus projection. 

Broadly speaking, Lilly yielded 0.6 percentage point of its obesity market share to Novo during the previous week, but still maintained its share level above 60%, according to Citi. 

In the recently launched Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, Lilly is capturing 7 out of 10 patients, with many on its Zepbound, Ricks told CNBC. Foundayo, according to Ricks, is attracting Medicare patients looking for convenience but not necessarily a huge weight-loss effect. 

UPDATED: Sept. 18, 2026

As expected, the past U.S. Labor Day holiday took a toll on obesity drugs' prescription numbers. According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, weekly scripts for Novo's Wegovy pill dropped roughly 12% sequentially to about 161K for the last week. The decline for Foundayo was modest, at just 1%, as the Lilly drug still managed to rake in more than 47K scripts. 

Lilly this week said Foundayo captured more than 30% of new patients in the U.S. market for oral obesity ​treatments, Reuters reported. 

Citing Bloomberg Symphony data, Jefferies analysts suggested in a Friday note that Foundayo's recent acceleration "has been driven primarily by retail/commercial channels."

Elsewhere, Lilly's total Zepbound scripts were down 8.5% week over week, but the GIP/GLP-1 drug expanded its market share by 0.4% versus Novo's Wegovy franchise, whose scripts decreased 10% during the period.

UPDATED: Sept. 11, 2026

Both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo saw their highest total prescriptions so far over the past week as the companies’ oral obesity battle continues to play out.  

According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, the Wegovy pill reached an approximate 183K total scripts for the most recent reporting period, versus 181K the week prior. Foundayo, for its part, climbed nearly 8% to reach 47.5K scripts. Citi analysts emphasized that IQVIA may still be missing some Foundayo prescriptions made through telehealth channels. 

Meanwhile, using the last four weeks as a guide, total GLP-1 prescriptions have increased by 5.4%, compared to a 6.8% decline the prior year, the Citi team said. Citi analysts attributed the 12-percentage-point swing to the expansion of oral GLP-1 therapies, which is likely broadening access to the class and drawing in new patients.  

Across the broader landscape, Lilly’s tirzepatide currently holds a nearly 57% share of the total GLP-1 market, compared to around 49.5% last year, while Novo’s semaglutide has stayed relatively flat at a 37% share, the analysts added.  

UPDATED: Sept. 4, 2026

Total prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo both grew over the past week, reaching roughly 181K (+3%) and 44K (+8%), IQVIA data showed, as cited by Citi. Both numbers are the two meds' highest so far. 

While Foundayo has yet to catch up with the Wegovy pill, the market share gap between the two oral drugs is slowly narrowing. According to an Aug. 28 Jefferies note based on data the previous week, Foundayo's share of new prescriptions (NRx), which exclude refills, was 21.5% in the oral obesity market.

Back to the most recent week, the Wegovy pill's position within the Wegovy family remained stable at 35%, as total Wegovy scripts increased 2.7% sequentially to 513.5K. During the same period, Lilly's Zepbound scripts climbed 1.6% to a little fewer than 772K.  

UPDATE: Aug. 28, 2026

Twenty weeks into its launch, Eli Lilly's Foundayo has finally exceeded 40,000 in weekly prescriptions, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 drug posted 40,862 scripts last week, bouncing back from a small dip the week prior. Still, the drug's scripts level is no match for the roughly 57K that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill garnered at week 6 of its own launch.

In its 33rd week of launch, the Wegovy pill booked roughly 175K scripts, slightly down from 176K, per IQVIA. The share of the oral version of semaglutide in all Wegovy obesity scripts was flat week over week at 35%. All told, across the pill and the injectable, Wegovy's weekly scripts were a little over 500K, down 0.8% sequentially.

As Jefferies analysts observed in an Aug. 21 note, Wegovy has been relatively flat since the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program began July 1.

Overall, the roughly 60%-40% obesity market share split between Lilly and Novo remained stable, as Lilly's Zepbound held its ground as the most popular drug.

UPDATE: Aug. 21, 2026

After a one-week hiccup, Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill regained its momentum last week with its largest prescription rate since it was launched in January. There were more than 176,000 prescriptions for the pill in the period, according to data gathered by IQVIA and cited in a note by Citi. 

The oral treatment now accounts for 35% of total Wegovy prescriptions, which is up from 33% the previous week, analysts from Citi said in their weekly update to investors.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo, which had been on a steady five-week climb, backtracked, with a drop-off from 38,928 prescriptions in the prior period to 36,620 in the latest week.

The movements for the two oral treatments contributed to overall market share adjustments for the companies' diabetes and obesity medicines. While Lilly made a 0.1% gain to 56.7%, Novo increased its market share by 0.3% to 37.1%.  

UPDATE: Aug. 14, 2026

Despite its leading position in the oral GLP-1 market, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill seems to be hitting a market share ceiling. For months now, shares of total prescriptions for Wegovy pill within the entire Wegovy franchise have struggled to break through the one-third mark.

While share of oral semaglutide within all Wegovy scripts hit 35% in our previous update, it fell back to 33% last week, as Wegovy pill scripts dropped to about 163K, down from a high of roughly 172K the week prior, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

Total Wegovy scripts, including the original injectable, declined 1.1% sequentially to about 495.5K. As a result, Novo yielded about 0.7 percentage point in obesity market share to Eli Lilly's Zepbound last week based on the IQVIA data. The split stood at 39.9% and 60.1% between Novo and Lilly.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo continued its upward trajectory with 38,928 total scripts, representing another step up from its previous record of 34,219 set the week prior.

UPDATE: Aug. 7, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo continue to build, jumping 16% sequentially to 34,219 the previous week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 med has been on a roll lately as it appears to celebrate four weeks of consecutive growth in total scripts. However, as Citi noted, there's still a potential gap in IQVIA's capture of telehealth data, and it's not clear how much of the scripts growth was from IQVIA getting better at including those data, or, if the actual growth was much faster in telehealth channels.

This week, Lilly's reported Foundayo sales for the second quarter—$98 million in total, including $67 million in the U.S.—disappointed many. As CEO David Ricks noted on an earnings call, Lilly began broad direct-to-consumer marketing to raise consumer awareness after securing commercial access across the three major pharmacy benefit managers in June. Besides, The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program went live on July 1, offering coverage for certain weight-loss medications, including Foundayo, for a $50 copayment per month. Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, said the company is "starting to see an inflection point on Foundayo now."

As for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill, total scripts recorded by IQVIA have been largely flat with small upticks in the past two weeks, having reached roughly 172K in the previous week. The oral version of semaglutide now makes up 35% of total Wegovy scripts, which take up about 40.6% of the U.S. obesity market share, as Lilly's Zepbound remains the leader. 

UPDATE: July 31, 2026

The small inflection point we noticed two weeks ago regarding Eli Lilly's Foundayo does not appear to be a flash in the pan. Weekly total prescriptions for the small molecule reached 29,388, a new high for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist after three weeks of consecutive growth, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

As IQVIA may be missing some scripts from telehealth channels, we will get a clearer picture of Foundayo's launch progress when Lilly reports its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday, Aug. 5. Analysts at Jefferies have been modeling $71 million in U.S. sales for the quarter based on IQVIA data.

Meanwhile, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill remains far ahead in the oral GLP-1 race with total scripts also hitting a new record of about 171,700, according to Citi. The number represents 1.1% growth from its previous best recorded during the prior week.

Coincidentally, the entire GLP-1 class also saw its total scripts grow 1.1% sequentially across diabetes and obesity uses. Lilly's Zepbound regained some lost ground with total scripts up 1.9% week over week. That's compared to Wegovy, which now makes up 40.6% of the obesity market after a 0.2% sequential decline in total scripts. 

Novo reports earnings on the same day as Lilly, Aug. 5.

UPDATE: July 24, 2026

After a post-holiday lull, prescriptions for GLP-1s have more than bounced back. Weekly prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo reached new highs during the previous week, collecting 169,800 and 26,760, respectively, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The two oral drugs' previous records were about 161.5K and 24.3K, respectively. 

Other GLP-1 drugs also enjoyed a boost, as total GLP-1 scripts across obesity and diabetes increased 6.6% sequentially, according to Citi.

From the obesity front, scripts for Lilly's Zepbound rose 7.7% sequentially to about 710K. The GLP-1/GIP dual agonist conceded 0.6 percentage points of market share to Novo but remains ahead of the game with a 58.9% share. That's compared to a 10.5% week-over-week scripts expansion for Novo's Wegovy, which mounted to about 495.5K. In that basket, about 34% belonged to Wegovy pill.

UPDATE: July 17, 2026

Following the Independence Day holiday, the overall GLP-1 market was down 5.1% week over week as measured by total prescriptions across obesity and diabetes uses, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi.

In the obesity field specifically, total scripts for Eli Lilly's Zepbound shrank by 3.1% sequentially to a little below 660K, while Novo Nordisk's Wegovy dipped 4.4% to about 448.5K.

Against this backdrop, Lilly's oral Foundayo seemed to enjoy a small inflection point, with a total 24,303 scripts notably breaking away from its roughly 20K level in the prior five weeks.  

Meanwhile, joining the bigger trend, Wegovy pill scripts dropped to 147.5K during the week, versus about 153K the prior week or 161.5K at its peak. But the contribution of the oral version to the overall Wegovy scripts remained stable at around a third, per Citi's note. 

UPDATE: July 10, 2026

The launch of Eli Lilly’s Foundayo remains “muted,” with weekly prescriptions flat over the last five weeks, analysts from Jefferies said in a July 10 note. The analysis is based on data collected by IQVIA.

In the 13th week of Foundayo’s launch, IQVIA reported 19,550 prescriptions, down for the third straight week after peaking at Week 10 with 21,648 prescriptions. The figure also comes in significantly shy of the Week 13 launch of Novo’s Wegovy pill (more than 105K scripts) and Lilly’s injected obesity treatment Zepbound (59K), but ahead of Novo’s injected Wegovy (13K).

Meanwhile, weekly scripts for Wegovy pill ticked slightly upward sequentially to about 153K, although they still lag behind the drug’s peak of more than 161K.

Jefferies points out that CVS was the last of the big three PBMs to provide coverage of Foundayo, starting on June 1. By contrast, Wegovy had full coverage at the first week of its launch.

While Jefferies’ $71 million quarterly sales projection for Foundayo sits significantly below Wall Street consensus of $130 million, the team still believes that the Lilly med can reach the consensus revenue estimate of $1.2 billion for 2026.

UPDATE: July 6, 2026

For a month now, weekly prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo have been hovering at around 20,000. In other words, three months into its market debut, the non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist was still at the same script level that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill had achieved in two to three weeks post-launch.

For the week ended on June 26, Foundayo's total scripts dipped about 4% sequentially to 19,830, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. During the same period, scripts were also down about 2% for oral Wegovy, reaching about 149,000.

In a July 4 report, Jefferies analysts modeled about $71 million in U.S. sales during Foundayo's debut quarter from April to June, versus the team's previous estimate of $85 million in a June 26 report. Wall Street's consensus currently has the number at $130 million. To reach its estimate, Jefferies used an illustrative calculation based on the IQVIA data, with certain assumptions regarding pricing, dosing and stocking.

While Lilly still lags Novo on the oral GLP-1 battlefield, the Indianapolis pharma has maintained a majority 59.5% share of the overall obesity market, according to IQVIA's prescription data.  

As Novo's injectable Wegovy gained about 0.2% scripts (roughly 500) to reach 315,000 for the period, Lilly's Zepbound expanded by 1%, including 375,000 (+3,500) from Zepbound autoinjector and 289,000 (+2,000) from Zepbound DTC Vial+KwikPen.

UPDATE: June 29, 2026

Likely thanks to the Juneteenth federal holiday, prescriptions for both Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo were lower compared with their highest. For the week ended on June 19, Foundayo logged 20,594 total scripts, down from 21,648 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. 

For oral Wegovy, the numbers were about 152,000 for the June 19 week, a roughly 9,500 (5.9%) decrease from the prior week. 

As Jefferies' analysts noted, most GLP-1 scripts were down or rather flat in their weekly comparisons. Injectable Wegovy added about 1,000 (0.3%) scripts, landing at 315,000. Mounjaro essentially saw no change, at 804,000.

Lilly has previously noted that it takes time to build awareness for Foundayo as a new brand, whereas Novo benefits from familiarity with the Wegovy moniker. 

Meanwhile, Sandoz just announced that the FDA has accepted its generic tirzepatide autoinjector applications, covering all indications of Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound. We'll see how the availability of a generic injectable version shakes up the oral market. 

UPDATE: June 18, 2026

Name recognition and "familiarity" with Novo Nordisk's oral Wegovy has contributed to its rapid uptake in its battle with Lilly's oral GLP-1 Foundayo, according to Spherix analyst Jim Hickey, who conducts monthly surveys with doctors who prescribe the treatments. See Fierce's story on Hickey's analysis here.

UPDATE: June 12, 2026

The share of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill among total Wegovy scripts appears to have reached a plateau, hovering around one-third over the past few weeks. The latest number for the week ended on June 5 was 33%, compared with 30%, 32% and 31% in the prior weeks, according to Citi. 

Meanwhile, the obesity market share split between Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound has been relatively stable at around 40% to 42%, as the Indianapolis pharma's oral Foundayo makes up only a small portion of the market even though its own scripts continue to build. 

Wegovy's total scripts were up 9.8% on a weekly basis, reaching nearly 484,500. Within this haul, Wegovy pill contributed roughly 159,000, the oral version's highest since its launch. The drug's previous highest was 146,000 before dipping to 134,000 in our last update.

Zepbound's scripts also grew week over week by 9.3%, nearing 667,400 for the week. During the same period, IQVIA tracked slightly shy of 20,000 scripts from Foundayo in its ninth week on the market, compared with nearly 17,000 the prior week. 

Thanks to the expansion of the oral version, Wegovy overall now commands 42.1% of the obesity market. Tracing backwards, its share has been climbing steadily, clocking in at 41.9%, 41.2%, 41.4%, 40.5%, 40.4%, 42.6% and 40.4% in the past few weeks.

UPDATE: June 8, 2026

It took just over five months for Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill to log 3 million total U.S. prescriptions, underscoring “one of the strongest US pharmaceutical launches by volume on record,” the company announced in a June 7 press release. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s rival Foundayo has still yet to achieve more than 17,000 prescriptions, according to a June 5 note from Citi analysts.  

Using data from IQVIA, the analysts tracked 16,982 Foundayo prescriptions as of the drug's eighth week on the market since its April launch. However, the Citi team emphasizes that “there may be a gap in telehealth capture,” as Lilly has previously confirmed to the analysts around 20,000 Foundayo scripts since its launch. Foundayo has been floating around this range for several weeks now since hitting 16,698 at week six, the data show.

Meanwhile, Novo’s Wegovy pill was at 73,544 prescriptions by the time it had hit the same eight-week marker in its own launch. The drug had picked up one million prescriptions 12 weeks after launching and nabbed an additional two million prescriptions in the following ten weeks, Novo said in its release. At its three million total, one prescription is filled roughly every five seconds, the company pointed out in its release. 

Either way, IQVIA’s data suggests a preference for oral formulations in the wider GLP-1 market, with oral Wegovy prescriptions now contributing 30% of total Wegovy scripts, according to the Citi analysts. The oral offering may be driving a wider market for the obesity treatments as well, with Novo explaining in its recent release that more than 80% of its new prescriptions for the Wegovy pill come from people new to GLP-1 therapy. 

June 2 findings from Spherix Global Insights second the notion that oral GLP-1 pills are expanding the overall treatment pool and drawing in a “massive wave of new patients,” the company said in an emailed release. In oral Wegovy’s first four weeks on the market earlier this year, 73% of surveyed primary care physician reported prescribing the med, with over 98% who haven’t yet prescribed it planning to within the next six months, Spherix found. 

“Novo Nordisk’s early performance has set an exceptionally high bar for the competition,” Spherix’s gastroenterology franchise head, Jim Hickey, commented.

On a weekly basis, however, total GLP-1 prescriptions were trending downward over the week of June 1, falling 5.7% week-over-week, Citi analysts noted. Other than the continued rollout of Lilly and Novo’s respective weight loss pills, the analysts cited the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies as a key future event that they think could impact total prescriptions. 

UPDATE: June 1, 2026

In its seventh week on the market, which ended May 22, Eli Lilly’s obesity pill Foundayo continued to track below the pace of Novo Nordisk’s rival Wegovy pill at the same point in its launch.

At the same time, analysts at Jefferies and Citi again flagged caveats that could be skewing the numbers, with the Jefferies team espousing confidence that Lilly’s oral GLP-1 can still meet consensus sales projections for both the second quarter and 2026 as a whole. 

Breaking down the numbers, the Jefferies team put seventh-week total Foundayo prescriptions lower versus the previous week at roughly 11,700, with the clarification that the data’s source, IQVIA, had to use a “best-estimate” tally for the latest week’s prescription trends. 

That trend remains “numerically lower” than the course charted by Novo’s Wegovy pill, which racked up an impressive 67,000 prescriptions in its seventh week, although Foundayo’s performance still tracks ahead of Novo’s injectable Wegovy and Lilly’s first obesity incretin med Zepbound at the same point in their respective rollouts, the analyst team said. 

Lilly has suggested it expects the market for oral obesity meds to “develop over time” and has also cited the time needed to build new brand awareness for Foundayo, according to Jefferies, which added that the Lilly pill’s commercial reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly” compared to oral Wegovy. Lilly has confirmed that coverage of Foundayo through CVS Caremark, the United States’ biggest PBM, will begin this week. 

Despite those apparent growing pains, the analysts at Jefferies called Foundayo’s ability to meet consensus sales estimates in the near-term and for the full year as “doable.” The analysts currently predict that Lilly’s oral weight loss med will garner $145 million in the second quarter on the way to a $1.6 billion haul for the full year. 

Consensus estimates are tracking for Q2 and full-year Foundayo sales of $136 million and $1.2 billion, respectively, according to Jefferies. 

On that note, analysts at Citi, have repeatedly warned that IQVIA’s prescription data may be failing to account for telehealth referrals, citing comments from Lilly executives on the total patients they were tracking as of the company’s Q1 earnings call. For its part, Citi placed the total number of Foundayo scripts for the week ending May 22 at roughly 16,000, based on the IQVIA stats. 

By comparison, Novo’s Wegovy pill clocked some 146,000 total scripts over that same seven-day stretch, per Citi. Citi once more flagged that Novo’s Wegovy pill is making up a growing portion of overall semaglutide obesity prescriptions, which the team said points to “preferences for oral formulations.”

UPDATE: May 22, 2026

With both Novo Nordisk’s and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1s establishing their footing in the U.S. obesity market, the companies’ respective Wegovy pill and orforglipron tablet Foundayo are making their mark on prescription trends for a class previously confined primarily to injectables.

Looking at the past four weeks, total U.S. GLP-1 prescriptions were up 3.6%, compared to 1.8% at the same time last year, analysts at Citi wrote in a Friday note to clients, citing script tracking data from IQVIA. The Citi team attributed that momentum to the ability of Novo’s and Lilly’s new oral launches to “broaden and reshape the market” for obesity incretin drugs.

As of the week ended May 15, IQVIA logged nearly 17,000 prescriptions for Lilly’s Foundayo, which debuted on April 9. As in prior weeks, the Citi analysts caveated that IQVIA’s data may be missing key prescribing stats from telehealth channels, flagging Lilly executives’ comments during an earnings call at the end of last month that there were then roughly 20,000 patients on the new oral therapy.

Conversely, Novo’s Wegovy pill has recorded roughly 142,000 prescriptions as of last week, according to Citi’s note.

In an apparent sign of the new oral option's popularity, the analysts flagged that oral Wegovy now comprises 31% of total prescriptions for the brand, which is otherwise administered as an injection. The Citi team noted that this trend could signal “preferences for oral formulations.”

Meanwhile, scoping out the broader U.S. GLP-1 market over the past four weeks, Lilly’s tirzepatide brand—which includes both Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes—now holds a 54.8% share compared to a 47% piece of the pie last year. Novo’s U.S. market share for semaglutide has remained “relatively flat” over that stretch and clocked in at 37.4%, per Citi.

Week over week, total GLP-1 prescriptions were down a little less than 1% in the U.S. Looking at obesity specifically, Citi’s analysts flagged a 2.1% tirzepatide prescription decline versus last week, while Novo’s Wegovy prescriptions tracked at a positive 1.8%.

Aside from both companies' oral GLP-1 launches continuing to add texture to the market, the analysts noted that the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies on Novo’s and Lilly’s drugs could boost overall prescriptions for the class. 

UPDATE: May 15, 2026

Total prescriptions for Eli Lilly’s Foundayo reached 10,248 for the week that ended May 8, up from 7,335 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. While still on the rise, Foundayo’s growth pace continued to lag behind that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill during the same stage of their launch. 

Wegovy’s total scripts rose by 1.3% week over week to nearly 446,000, as its share in the obesity GLP-1 market climbed 0.1 percentage point to 40.5%, according to Citi.

However, Wegovy’s growth apparently didn’t come from its oral formulation. Wegovy pill scripts landed at about 137,000 for the week, down from roughly 143,000 the prior week, marking the first time that the pill's scripts have fallen since the oral launch in early January.

Scripts from the Wegovy pill made up 31% of total Wegovy scripts for the period, down 2 percentage points from the previous week. Still, Citi analysts argued that this roughly one-third of share “suggests preferences for oral formulations.”

Even as Wegovy gained ground, Lilly’s Zepbound remained the obesity market leader, with 59.5% share, as its nearly 656,000 scripts marked 0.8% growth week over week. 

UPDATE: May 8, 2026

As Eli Lilly’s Foundayo finds its footing on the market, Novo Nordisk’s own Wegovy pill—which got a three-month head start to launch over its rival this year—is starting to illuminate just how significant an oral GLP-1 may be to the lucrative obesity drug landscape. 

In the fourth week since its April 9 debut in the U.S., Lilly’s Foundayo has generated 7,335 total prescriptions, analysts at Citi wrote in a note to clients Friday, citing prescribing stats from IQVIA. 

That ramp-up looks slower on paper than that enjoyed by the Wegovy pill during its initial rollout, but the Citi team cautioned that there may be a gap in IQVIA data linked to telehealth prescriptions for Lilly’s tablet. They pointed to comments from Lilly executives late last week indicating that there were now some 20,000 patients on Foundayo, with the company noting that telehealth platforms were generating some 35% of the oral GLP-1 medicine’s current launch volume. 

The analysts acknowledged that Lilly’s early Foundayo prescription trends “continue to build,” while adding that they “look for further growth to develop the oral competitive market.” 

During its earnings call last week, Lilly added that upcoming coverage secured at major pharmacy benefit managers should come online by the middle of May, providing a likely sizeable tailwind to Foundayo’s trajectory. 

As for Novo, the company logged some 440,410 Wegovy prescriptions on the week that ended May 1, with oral Wegovy now making up 33% of those total obesity referrals, per the Citi analysts, who said that trend could reflect “preferences for oral formulations.”

The update on the oral obesity numbers comes after Novo earlier this week reported that the Wegovy pill generated 2.26 billion Danish kroner (around $355 million) in its first quarter on the U.S. market. 

For its part, Foundayo will likely need to start generating around 22,000 prescriptions a week in order to hit current consensus forecasts of $160 million in second-quarter sales, RBC Capital Markets’ Trung ​Huynh said this week, as cited by Reuters. 

UPDATE: May 4, 2026

With three weeks of data on Lilly’s oral GLP-1 launch in obesity now on the books, the dimensions of Foundayo’s rollout—and its critical comparison to that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill—are coming into focus. 

In its third week on the U.S. market, which ended April 24, Foundayo generated some 5,600 prescriptions, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a May 1 note to clients. That level of adoption is numerically lower than the stats recorded by the Wegovy pill in its third week, when prescriptions for the oral obesity med came in at around 26,100, per the note. 

Nevertheless, almost all of Foundayo’s recorded performance stems from cash pay channels, according to the Jefferies team, with commercial access via insurance set to come online by the middle of this month, which will likely give Foundayo a substantial boost in uptake. 

The team acknowledged that Foundayo’s reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly vs oral Wegovy’s.” 

Overall, the analysts described Foundayo as “off to a solid start,” and estimate the drug will generate $146 million in the second quarter and $1.6 billion for all of 2026. That compares to consensus forecasts of $134 million and $1.2 billion, respectively. 

Lilly told the Jefferies team that, as of week three of its launch, some 45% of Foundayo prescriptions were coming through its direct-to-patient channel LillyDirect, alongside 35% of referrals from telehealth providers and the remaining 20% coming from traditional retail venues. 

During an earnings call with analysts last week, Lilly executives noted that there were around 20,000 patients on Foundayo in the U.S. The drug was approved April 1. 

As for Novo’s pill, oral Wegovy lassoed around 135,000 total prescriptions during the week that ended April 24, according to the Jefferies notes. 

UPDATE: April 24, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 obesity treatment Foundayo has attracted 3,707 prescriptions though its second week on the market, lagging far behind the pace of Novo Nordisk’s GLP-1 pill Wegovy, which drew 18,410 prescriptions though its second week on the market in January. 

The results were made available by Jefferies from healthcare analytics firm IQVIA and are good through the week ending on April 17.

With the result, Lilly’s shares dipped by 4% on Friday, compared to a 7% gain for Novo.

Foundayo’s launch so far does compare favorably to that of Novo’s injected Wegovy, which numbered 1,578 prescriptions through two weeks when it reached the market in the U.S. but falls short of Lilly’s Zepbound pen, which counted 7,292 prescriptions through its second week.

In its note to investors, analysts from Jefferies called the result “disappointing vs. expectations."

Brand recognition has played a role, according to Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen, who said that online searches for GLP-1 drugs peaked during Wegovy’s launch, potentially boosting demand.

UPDATE: April 21, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo is off to a solid launch, drawing 1,390 prescriptions in its first week on the market, according to tracking figures from IQVIA and presented by Jefferies. The tabulation is from the week starting April 6. This compares to the 3,071 prescriptions Novo Nordisk garnered during its Wegovy pill launch week in January.

While Foundayo came up short in this oral GLP-1 launch week comparison, it did exceed the number of prescriptions recorded in the first week of the launch of both Lilly’s injected Zepbound (1,100) and Novo’s injected version of Wegovy (768).

In a note to clients, analysts with Jefferies cautioned that comparisons can be “tricky” given that oral Wegovy was launched at the start of the year and that initial capture rates from IQVIA are “volatile” and may not include product sampling. 

“Overall, we think Foundayo’s initial scripts look excellent,” the Jefferies team wrote, adding that it is modeling Foundayo’s sales to reach $1.6 billion this year, compared to a consensus of $1.5 billion, with its peak annual sales topping out at $30 billion versus the consensus of $26 billion. 

“We think the real opportunity for Foundayo is ex-U.S., given its clear advantages on scale, distribution and [cost of goods sold],” Jefferies wrote.

data.title: AZ enlists former teen TV star for biomarker testing push
data.description:
Time out: “Saved by the Bell” actor Mark-Paul Gosselaar is the new face (and name) of AstraZeneca’s biomarker testing push, “Meet Your Mark.”

In a nostalgic campaign that plays on Gosselaar’s “time out” catchphrase from the 1989 teen sitcom, the actor helps AZ spread the word about the importance of biomarker testing in cancer care as a “warm, relatable guide," the company explained in an Oct. 28 press release. 

Biomarker testing can clue oncologists into what kind of therapies may help a person's specific cancer and determine how aggressive it is, among other important signals. Such testing is recommended for several cancers including lung, breast and prostate cancer. In a 1,200-person study, more than 75% of people affected by cancer who had biomarker testing agreed that it gave their doctor valuable information to help guide their treatment plan, AZ noted in its announcement. 

However, only about one-third of people with advanced cancer in the U.S. undergo that testing, despite its inclusion in established medical guidelines.  

“Having seen loved ones navigate cancer diagnoses, I felt it was important to spread the word about biomarker testing,” Gosselaar commented in the company release. “By bringing back my history of calling a ‘time out’, we’re empowering those living with cancer to take a moment to ask their doctor about biomarker testing, enabling them to play a more active role in their care.”

In a three-minute video that accompanies the campaign, Gosselaar listens in on a conversation between diner patrons about treatment options for prostate cancer, looking straight at the camera with a knowing glance before deploying his classic “Saved by the Bell” fourth wall break with a “time out” gesture. 

“Cool. Still works,” he says, acknowledging the nostalgic call-back.

Related

Cologuard campaign reunites ‘Full House’ stars to give ‘The Talk’ about colon cancer screening

As the scene comes back to life with the snap of Gosselaar’s fingers, the video leans into the humor of his abrupt intrusion into the patron’s booth: “And you came from where?” the woman whose conversation was interrupted quips. The theme follows throughout the video as the actor continues to pop into unsuspecting patrons' conversations after freezing the scene with a "time out." 

Gosselaar goes on to explain what biomarkers are and how biomarker testing can help better inform specific treatment plans. While the couple at the booth ponders “where do I know that guy from,” AZ’s new biomarker mouthpiece is already off to spread the word to another diner patron, who is talking on the phone about breast cancer. 

After Gosselaar tells the confused young woman to make sure her Aunt Emily gets biomarker testing, next up is a conversation about lung cancer occurring at another booth. In this case, the new patient’s doctor has already ordered a biomarker test. Gosselaar confirms that a biomarker test is the “appropriate next step” before talking directly into the camera to point viewers to AZ’s campaign website to learn more. 

The website offers more information and resources to walk people through the process of asking for and receiving biomarker testing. AZ also showcases several real patient stories on the site, as well as a doctor who further explains why patients should “Meet Your Mark.” 

“At AstraZeneca, our goal is to one day eliminate cancer as a cause of death. We believe biomarker testing has a critical role to play in making this possible by providing doctors with valuable insights to guide cancer care,” the company’s head of U.S. oncology Mohit Manrao explained in a statement. “Through Meet Your Mark and our partnership with Mark-Paul Gosselaar, we’re calling attention to biomarkers as a powerful tool in navigating a cancer diagnosis, supporting our broader commitment to cancer care.”

With precision medicine a continued focus across many oncology drugmakers such as AstraZeneca, biomarker testing is increasingly important to ensure that drugs across AZ’s portfolio can reach the appropriate patients. 

Using a familiar, nostalgic voice to drum up interest toward that goal is a familiar tactic, seen recently in Cologuard’s colorectal cancer screening campaign that brought back Jodie Sweetin and John Stamos from the hit 90’s sitcom “Full House." Meanwhile, Bayer recently went with former teenage witch Melissa Joan Hart for its menopause awareness push.

data.title: Women 'still waiting' to trust healthcare institutions: report
data.description:
After decades of being put on the backburner, women across the U.S. are “still waiting” to trust healthcare systems, a new report finds. 

Langrand, a women-led healthcare strategy firm, sought to find out what women’s trust in healthcare looks like today through its 2026 Women’s Health Report, “Still Waiting.” Through survey responses from 1,000 women between the ages of 18 and 44, the Oct. 28 report details “what it will take to earn that trust, and what it costs to keep women waiting."

“I expected frustration for sure,”  Langrand’s CEO and founder, Shannon Langrand said in an interview. “I didn't quite expect how behavioral it had become.”

According to the research, 73% of women surveyed have felt dismissed or not taken seriously by providers due to their gender, with 34% of that group remarking that this occurs “frequently.” 

As the report points out, U.S. healthcare systems have a long, dark history of actively dismissing women, from the broad diagnosis of “hysteria” that was applied to women in the 1800s to the 1977 FDA guidance that kept women “of childbearing potential” out of early-stage drug trials until 1993. Even in 2024, women who report the same pain levels of men in an emergency treatment setting are less likely to be prescribed pain meds, the report points out. 

Although “hysteria” as a blanket term for women’s symptoms isn’t something likely to be heard in a doctor’s office today, it isn’t uncommon for women’s concerns to be brushed off as hormonal or anxiety related. In fact, eight in 10 women surveyed reported having had their symptoms labeled as “stress, anxiety or hormonal,” while four in 10 (42%) hear that reaction “often,” the report found. 

This can lead to misdiagnoses or delayed diagnoses. 33% of women surveyed have experienced a misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis, a problem especially pronounced in the mental health, chronic pain, reproductive, autoimmune and cardiovascular realms. For serious health issues such as these, misdiagnoses can lead to dangerous consequences. For example, women are 50% more likely than men to receive the wrong diagnosis after a heart attack, the report notes, citing data from a study funded in part by the British Heart Foundation. 

The history and continued reality of this dismissiveness hampers trust for women, with only 140 of the 1,000 (14%) women surveyed reporting that they “fully trust” traditional healthcare intuitions to understand their needs. 

As the research shows, those who are skeptical have nowhere else to go; 38% noted that they “trust no alternative” to traditional healthcare. This plays into real-world behavior, as 44% of women note that they “occasionally” skip or delay care due to cost, inconvenience or distrust, while 33% do the same “frequently.” 

While cost is the top reasoning for this choice, one in three women attributed delaying care to prior negative experiences that make them hesitate to seek care again. 

Related

Women’s ‘new health ecosystem’ takes shape on Reddit: report

The findings also suggest that barriers like cost are not a “fixed” ceiling, as 52% of women surveyed said that they would “maybe” pay out of pocket for women-focused services and 28% replied that “yes,” they would. This speaks to part of the reason Langrand dug into this research. 

“There’s a lot of attention on women” right now, the CEO observed, pointing to, in part, a rising popularity in women’s sports. At the same time, she noticed women being even “less willing than they once were to keep adapting themselves to systems that weren’t really designed around them."

“Healthcare keeps asking patients to navigate complexity that healthcare created,” Langrand said in an interview. “What we're seeing is that women are beginning to route themselves and their families around that.”

 

“Embarrassingly basic” solutions

 

Beyond brick-and-mortar institutions and in-person HCP visits, health information on social media is trusted by some, although 47% of women surveyed report that they still trust doctors more than information distributed on platforms such as TikTok, Instagram and YouTube. Eighteen percent, however, hold an “equal trust” for both doctors and social media. 

For the most part (40%), women turn to social media for validation, not information, suggesting that feeling heard and seen is something they may be lacking from their providers, Langrand's research suggests. 

To bring women back to traditional healthcare, providers may need to adapt their messaging and communication to women’s needs. The report offers tips such as leading with listening, acknowledging the history of barriers to women in healthcare and removing stigma by treating “asking for help as ordinary.” 

To that point, “being listened to by clinicians” was the top answer (20%) when women were asked what would rebuild their trust the fastest, while “care that remembers me as a person” came in next with 17% of responses. 

“The challenges outlined in this report are big ones," the report emphasized. "The fixes women ask for are not." 

The solutions to rebuilding trust, Langrand said, are “almost embarrassingly basic” and could get even simpler when factoring in new technological advances such as artificial intelligence. As it stands, AI is largely used to help bolster operational efficiency in healthcare, but there’s still room for AI innovation to instead be used to help “meet that woman where she is” and create a more “human experience,” she suggested. 

Related

Real Chemistry spotlights health dignity as key trust, engagement indicator in new research initiative

Importantly, women’s frustrations with the healthcare system hold weight beyond the individual. Seventy-seven percent of the women surveyed in the report make the healthcare decisions for their household, a key consideration when coupled with the research’s findings on behavioral changes such as delaying care or switching providers.

“I believe the industry should pay attention to that,” Langrand said. “When women walk, they are taking their influence over healthcare and the dollars that represents with them, and I think that’s something that the industry has not paid attention to very much.”

data.title: GSK vows not to ‘park crap on Page 41’ in transparency push
data.description:
GSK's chief executive Luke Miels has committed to a transparent communication strategy after telling analysts during its Q3 financial call that “we are not going to park crap on Page 41 of a press release and hope none of you notice it.”

Miels became GSK CEO back in January. During his latest earnings call, Miels took the opportunity to make a high-level point about how he wants to communicate with the owners of the company, analysts and the market more broadly. Miels rejected the strategy of burying bad news deep in GSK’s corporate communications. 

“Look, we are going to call things as we see them,” Miels said. “We will tell you as much as we can. We will have a plan to address it. Please, just adjust your parameters on that because that’s how we want to operate. All right?” 

The CEO made the comment while answering a question about leadership changes at ViiV Healthcare, GSK's HIV business. Last week, ViiV revealed that its CEO, Deborah Waterhouse, is leaving the company to take the top job at CSL. ViiV has promoted Lynn Baxter, currently president of GSK Europe, to replace Waterhouse. 

As an analyst noted on the earnings call, the CEO change followed the departure of ViiV's chief financial officer and head of R&D earlier this year. The analyst asked if the leadership changes are connected and whether GSK is rebooting its HIV business under Miels. 

The CEO rejected the suggestion that the changes are connected, explaining that R&D chief Kimberly Smith retired and that Waterhouse received the sort of promotion offer that doesn’t “come along every day.” Miels said he wants ViiV “to be closer and so there will be more intensive interaction and supervision there, but that is not a bad thing.”

data.title: GSK talks through Hibsago launch as it reports out mixed Q3
data.description:
Armed with a trio of recent high-profile approvals, GSK is banking on its specialty medicines to drive its next wave of growth, even as investor enthusiasm cooled Wednesday morning amid reports of restructuring charges and a vaccine sales dip at the British drugmaker.

The company’s most recent green light came by way of Hibsago, an antisense oligonucleotide bringing the promise of a functional cure for the first time for certain patients with chronic hepatitis B virus infection. 

With regulatory go-aheads now locked down in the U.S. and Japan, China is the next priority for GSK. The company’s president of global product strategy, Nina Mojas, noted on a conference call that the three countries comprise “around 80% of the potential value for Hibsago.” 

Many analyst shops are pinning blockbuster expectations on Hibsago, with the team at Jefferies last week affirming a projection of 2.2 billion pounds sterling (around $3 billion) in potential peak sales opportunity. 

Both China and Japan have made treatment of hepatitis B a national priority, and in Japan, GSK has received a “very positive reimbursement decision” as doctors have “already identified patients to receive therapy,” Mojas added. 

Conversely, hepatitis B is “very concentrated” in the U.S., with most patients clustered in just five states, the GSK exec pointed out. 

“We have launched with a focus on patients with surface antigen level lower than 1,000,” Mojas said, referring to the detectable level of the virus in the blood, “where the opportunity to have a positive experience leading to functional cure is the highest.” 

Related

GSK vows not to ‘park crap on Page 41’ in transparency push

In GSK’s B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 trials that led to Hibsago’s approval, the medicine allowed 19% of patients in a broad population to achieve the program’s defined criteria for a functional cure, with that rate rising to 26% among patients with HBV surface antigen below the 1,000 international units per milliliter threshold at the trial’s start. 

The drug’s label specifically indicates Hibsago for patients who’ve been taking Nrtl therapy for at least six months, and who have suppressed hepatitis B virus DNA and virus surface antigen levels no greater than 3000 IU/ml. 

Following last week’s FDA nod, GSK now expects the medicine to become available in the U.S. within roughly the next 10 days, Mojas suggested on Wednesday. 

While the green light no doubt marks a foundational shift in hepatitis B treatment potential, safety and monitoring requirements tied to Hibsago do have the potential to “cause debate” about the medicine’s trajectory in real-world practice, the Jefferies team noted last week. 

In drawing attention to Hibsago’s black box warning for hepatic flares and thrombocytopenia, the Jefferies analysts noted that a weekly or every-other-week monitoring burden for patients could “work against the commercial uptake and could slow adoption outside specialist hepatology centers." 

Addressing those uncertainties on GSK’s third-quarter earnings call, Mojas said that those requirements are likely to “evolve” over the course of an individual’s treatment journey. 

“It’s quite important in the initial periods, and we do expect that physicians will monitor early, seeing if their patients are by any chance one of those who have early elevation of ALT or … severe thrombocytopenia,” she said. 

After that initial attention to potential safety flags, “we expect that physicians and patients could find some kind of balance of when and how frequently they do the monitoring,” she explained. 

Aside from Hibsago, GSK’s vanguard of new launches is further girded by the company’s first approved lung cancer medicine Jideytro—cleared by the FDA in July—and Jemperli, which recently picked up a first-in-class nod in a specific type of rectal cancer following a buzzy early trial readout. 

All three drugs form part of GSK’s specialty medicine roster, which did the bulk of the heavy lifting in the third quarter and grew sales by 15% to 3.9 billion pounds ($5.2 billion) with Cabenuva at the helm. 

The long-acting HIV treatment grew sales 35% during the period, with Mojas noting that “more than 75% of switches continue to come from competitors in the U.S.” She added that, as the current lone long-acting injectable HIV treatment, the drug has built out “a strong foundation with patients who prefer to take medicines less frequently.” 

This could in turn set up Cabenuva for further success in 2027, when data on a three-times-a-year formulation is due to read out, Mojas said. Cabenuva is currently approved in both once-monthly and every-other-month regimens. 

On the other end of the spectrum, vaccine sales slumped 2% in the quarter, “with the drag from Shingrix China destocking,” Mojas noted. 

That was countered somewhat by 12% growth in GSK’s meningitis portfolio, however. 

All told, GSK’s third-quarter sales worked out to 8.9 billion pounds (around $11.8 billion), good for 5% growth over the same period in 2025. 

Related

CSL taps GSK’s Deborah Waterhouse as CEO in darkest hour

Whether it can be credited to the vaccine results, or further details on GSK’s downsizing strategy and a newly reported 328 million pounds in Q3 charges related to its restructuring, investors didn’t react as warmly to the earnings news as the company might have hoped. As of late Wednesday morning, the British pharma’s stock was trading down around 3.38%. 

Looking forward, GSK stood by a number of its established targets in both the near- and medium-term. The company continues to expect overall sales growth between 3% and 5% this year, and it remains steadfast in its ambition to reach sales of more than 40 billion pounds ($53 billion) by 2031.

data.title: Consulting firm Blue Matter picks up comms agency Cognite
data.description:
Strategic consulting firm Blue Matter is boosting its communications digs with the acquisition of global healthcare communications agency Cognite. 

With a tagline of “bringing science to life,” Cognite primarily focuses on complex specialty markets such as rare diseases and offers services across commercial, medical, corporate and patient communications. Blue Matter, meanwhile, is a “valuable strategic resource and a thought leader” in biopharma portfolio, product and functional strategy,” CEO Ashwin Dandekar commented in an Oct. 28 press release.  

The firm has been “systemically bringing together” important communications and creative capabilities over the past few years to support its strategies with providers, payers, patients and other stakeholders, making Cognite’s “array of capabilities, creativity, and team culture” a “perfect fit for the Blue Matter family,” Dandekar added. 

Cognite houses its worldwide array of offices and people in London, England; Zug, Switzerland; and Boston, U.S., and looks to take its communications skills to a “far wider audience” as part of Blue Matter, its CEO Lee Hurley noted in a statement, pointing to the “tremendous opportunities for growth” stemming from the merger. 

“Our last decade of growth has demonstrated the appetite and belief in our proposition and how to deliver it,” Cognite’s chief business officer Sean Cush added. “Our focus on transformative medicines and the complex diseases they tackle is now something we can turbocharge by joining Blue Matter, harnessing world-class strategic capabilities, empowering technologies, and gaining true global reach.”

Related

Eversana combines forces with UK-based AI health economics research firm Estima in acquisition

No financial terms were disclosed for the deal. Blue Matter is a portfolio company of global private equity Biard Capital. 

While the M&A landscape across healthcare agencies has been hot recently, recent deals have largely focused on integrating AI and emerging tech capabilities. Eversana, for one, dove deeper into the global AI services pool with its Oct. 28 buy of London-based health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) company Estima Scientific, while CG Life picked up AI-native agency The Considered+AI over the summer.

data.title: Amgen hit with FDA warning letter for ‘misleading’ video
data.description:
Amgen has been handed an FDA warning letter over a video promoting its cancer drug Vectibix, but the company said the issues stemmed from an inadvertent submission.

Vectibix first won FDA approval back in 2006 for certain patients with advanced colorectal cancer. It has since picked up additional approvals for the disease, most recently in 2025 as a combination treatment with Amgen’s cancer drug Lumakras for patients with KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer who had previously received chemotherapy.

Vectibix carries a boxed warning for dermatologic toxicity, along with warnings about several other serious and potentially fatal risks, including infusion reactions, pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung disease.

But the FDA said a promotional video submitted by Amgen “entirely omits risk information.”

The agency said the video is “misleading” because it highlights the benefits of Vectibix but “fails to communicate any risk information.”

That omission “creates a misleading impression about the drug’s safety,” the regulator said in its warning letter, adding that “this omission is especially problematic from a public health perspective given the serious and potentially fatal risks associated with the drug.”

The FDA also said that while the Amgen video suggests Vectibix can be used to treat wild-type RAS metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) generally, it “does not specify that Vectibix is indicated in specific regimens based on its line in therapy.”

The video also failed to adequately communicate Vectibix's limitations of use, including restrictions involving patients with RAS-mutant mCRC or unknown RAS mutation status. As a result, the video “creates a misleading impression about the drug’s FDA-approved indication and use,” the FDA said.

The warning letter, issued by the FDA's Office of Prescription Drug Promotion, was dated Aug. 12 but only became public Oct. 27. Amgen was given 15 working days from receipt of the letter to respond to the agency's concerns, including outlining plans to address the alleged violations.

An Amgen spokesperson told Fierce: “An incorrect video file for a Vectibix advertisement was inadvertently submitted to FDA that did not contain the required risk information, but the file was never publicly disseminated.

“Amgen considers the appropriate communication of risk information to be of utmost importance in its promotional materials, and we take all concerns very seriously. The Vectibix advertisement that was publicly disseminated included the appropriate Important Safety Information, and we have submitted the correct file to the FDA.”

data.title: Supernus taps snowboarder Chloe Kim in new Qelbree push
data.description:
Supernus Pharmaceuticals is tasking Olympic snowboarder Chloe Kim with shredding down the mountain of misinformation and stigma surrounding women with ADHD in the latest chapter of its “Ms. Represented” marketing push for non-stimulant treatment Qelbree. 

Kim, a 26-year-old American snowboarder and two-time Olympic gold medalist, opens up about her journey navigating an ADHD diagnosis in her twenties. This includes finding a non-stimulant treatment that works for her lifestyle in Supernus’ new extension of its Qelbree campaign. Through a series of multi-channel and editorial content, Kim puts a new face to Supernus’ efforts to challenge stereotypes and spotlight the often-overlooked discrepancies in an ADHD diagnosis for women. 

Women can often present with inattentive symptoms as opposed to the more overt hyperactive symptoms of ADHD typically associated with boys and men, something that can “mask” these symptoms, meaning many women won’t see a diagnosis until adulthood, according to Supernus. In fact, more than 60% of U.S. women received their ADHD diagnosis in adulthood, compared to 40% of men. 

Supernus shed light on the challenges women with ADHD can face in last year’s initial “Ms. Represented” campaign with actress and Qelbree user Busy Phillips, who didn’t realize she had been living with ADHD until her daughter was diagnosed. With Kim now joining the “Ms. Represented” roster, the company hopes to reach an “even younger” audience of adult women, marketing VP Rebecca Lannan, who was named Marketer of the Year at the recent Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards, explained in an interview. 

Along with a dedicated campaign website, Kim and her story will be featured in a digital cover story for Gallery Media Group’s style brand Coveteur, which will touch on ADHD education while integrating Kim’s “very personal style” and creativity, Lannan noted. Meanwhile, Gallery Media Group’s women’s lifestyle publication PureWow will spotlight Kim and her Qelbree experience specifically in its “check-in” wellness franchise. 

The digital, social media-forward push will continue with Kim’s appearance in a video for Gen Z social media video publisher NowThis’s “Are You Okay?” interview series. 

In Kim’s “Are You Okay?” episode, the snowboarder will talk candidly in a conversational format that’s designed to “challenge the outdated perception” of ADHD in women, Lannan said.

Supernus’ Qelbree marketing and the “Ms. Represented” campaign “started a little bit grassroots, and now it’s really gained ground,” Lannan said. Now, as it looks to educate people across a spectrum of ages and demographics, the company is focusing on social channels such as Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat, where the younger audience is scrolling. 

Related

Supernus casts Busy Philipps as 'Ms. Represented' in Qelbree campaign targeting women with ADHD

“We want to capture them where they already are,” Lannan said, referring to the younger audience. 

While “Ms. Represented” focuses specifically on women, Supernus’ efforts to close the awareness diagnosis gap in ADHD spreads across genders, with Fox Sports NFL Insider Jay Glazer previously featured in a video series discussing his experience with ADHD and Qelbree. Knowing how both men and women experience ADHD differently is an important part of closing the diagnosis gap for the condition, Supernus emphasizes. 

“ADHD is a very prevalent condition, and it’s serious,” Lannan said. “And there’s stigma.” 

Qelbree won FDA approval to treat adults with ADHD in 2022, marking a significant expansion from its previous nod in children and unlocking a U.S. adult patient population of about 16 million. Last year, the med picked up $304.7 million in annual net product sales.

In the crowded ADHD treatment market, the drug stands out as a non-stimulant option. Compared to some of the giants in the ADHD space such as Takeda’s Adderall and Vyvanse (both of which have long gone generic), Qelbree isn’t categorized as a controlled substance in the U.S., a status that offers more flexibility for busy patients like Kim and Philips.

data.title: Eversana picks up London-based AI firm Estima Scientific
data.description:
Growing Eversana is tapping into the global AI services pool with a new acquisition, adding London-based health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) company Estima Scientific to its fold. 

The deal, for which financial terms are not disclosed, will see Estima integrate its specialist consulting expertise and proprietary software into Eversana’s established market access, value and evidence solutions to better help pharma companies prove their drug’s clinical and economic value “more efficiently and transparently” to payers, Eversana explained in an Oct. 28 release. 

Estima is bringing to the table an assortment of web-based, generative-AI applications that can bring “efficiency and accuracy” to economic modeling, systemic literature reviews, network meta-analysis and more. As Eversana notes, Estima’s solutions have already been validated by large pharma customers and leading health technology regulatory assessment bodies, including the U.K.’s National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). 

Eversana has been growing its commercialization digs since it merged with Waltz Health last summer, creating a combined healthcare platform with a joint mission of tackling “the industry’s misaligned incentives and fragmented patient experiences,” the companies said.

With now Estima on board as well, the company is further building on its efforts to “accelerate modernization” across the biopharma industry by joining technology-first solutions across its platform, it noted in the October release. 

Related

Lundbeck strikes expanded pact with Eversana to broaden AI scope across US commercial business

“Today more than ever, the pharmaceutical industry must embrace the power of AI to transform every element of commercialization,” Eversana’s CEO Mark Thierer commented. “As we scale to serve global clients, adding best-in-class companies that embrace a technology-first mindset is critical to our success.”

Estima’s team, which will join Eversana’s global workforce, “checks every box and will seamlessly fit into our value & evidence team, bringing game-changing solutions to drive market access success,” Thierer added. 

Estima was founded in 2019 and has since built a “strong base” of global clients that use its AI-powered tech to support research studies for global pharma brands. For Estima, joining Eversana is an “incredible milestone” and validates the “specialized technology and consulting expertise our team has built,” co-founder Tim Reason said. 

“The company’s global scale and end-to-end commercial infrastructure will allow us to accelerate how pharmaceutical companies build and communicate evidence-based value to payers, helping patients gain faster access to life-changing therapies,” Reason continued. 

Eversana, meanwhile, is all in on “pharmatizing AI,” Thierer told Fierce in an August interview. A year after unveiling its end-to-end AI agency platform in 2025, the company shook on an expanded pact with brain disease specialist Lundbeck this summer, allowing the latter to further “scale bionic capabilities responsibly across our commercial organization” and ultimately deliver greater value, Lundbeck’s U.S. EVP and president Tom Gibbs said at the time. 

With its AI capabilities, Eversana creates “a new way for pharma to do business, spanning marketing, sales, all the way through product launch,” Thierer said. “Pharmatizing AI is a competitive set of weapons for pharma to win market share, and in the end, get patients on the appropriate therapy.”

data.title: Lilly surges up diabetes reputation rankings to close in on Novo
data.description:
Eli Lilly has jumped up a ranking of the corporate reputations of diabetes drugmakers, putting it hot on the heels of Novo.

PatientView compiled the ranking by gathering the views of 71 diabetes patient groups in 30 countries. Asked to rank companies they work with, the patient groups put Novo in first place, followed by Lilly and Sanofi. Lilly and Sanofi swapped places in the ranking of companies that the diabetes groups are familiar with. Novo came top of both league tables. 

The Danish drugmaker is a familiar sight at the top of the rankings, having placed (PDF) first on both league tables last year. Lilly is a new arrival. Riding high on its GLP-1 medicines, Lilly climbed four places up the table of companies that groups work with. Lilly rose three places on the “familiar with” rankings. 

While Lilly has long been a force in the diabetes market, awareness of its brand has increased in recent years as the GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists Mounjaro and Zepbound have become household names and the company has embarked on corporate marketing campaigns. Against that backdrop, the company was the fastest riser up both of the PatientView diabetes league tables. 

The company climbed the diabetes rankings in a period when patient groups’ views of U.S. drugmakers in general soured. PatientView’s survey of patient groups across all therapeutic areas found volatility in reputations of drugmakers with large U.S. footprints. The recent volatility reflected political pressures and workforce reductions, PatientView said. 

Lilly’s ascent coincided with a slight uptick in overall perceptions of diabetes drugmakers. PatientView tracked improvements in diabetes groups’ views of the industry’s provision of patient information and approach to patient centricity.

However, perceptions of the industry’s activities in multiple areas fell over the same period. Innovation, transparency of clinical data and pricing, access to medicines, pharma integrity and fair pricing policies were among the areas where perceptions deteriorated.
